The disclosure comes amid a turbulent period for Nvidia, following Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation as CEO on November 12 and growing congressional scrutiny of the company's exposure to alleged Chinese chip-diversion schemes. Huang has agreed to answer questions from three House committees on December 1, with Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter scheduled to appear the following day.

In a post on X, Muddy Waters questioned whether a woman identified as Cenly Chen, and in some photograph tags as Cenly Puri, who has reportedly been photographed publicly with Puri between 2024 and 2026, is the same Cenly Chen formerly employed by Super Micro.

The short seller draws attention to an October 2026 consolidated class action complaint against Super Micro, which alleges that its former Chief Growth Officer Cenly Chen managed the company's acquisition of Nvidia GPUs and determined how they were distributed among customers. The complaint further alleges that Chen could not have been unaware of Super Micro's alleged illicit sales.

The allegations relate to a separate U.S. criminal case announced in March, involving three individuals associated with Super Micro who were indicted over an alleged scheme to sell approximately $2.5 billion of Nvidia-powered servers to end customers in China through a Southeast Asian front company.

Muddy Waters acknowledges that neither Cenly Chen nor Puri has been accused of criminal conduct by the government and that the allegations in the shareholder lawsuit remain unproven.

What Is Driving The Move In Super Micro Computer Stock?
Trefis Team

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) stock fell 33.1% between August 18 and November 16, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 3.3%. The fall ran through a stretch in which the company said, first in an October 20 update and then in its November 3 report, that its sales had come in well above its own guidance. The sharpest single-day sell-off came on November 12, when shares dropped 11.3% following a Bloomberg report that federal prosecutors are investigating whether third-party entities diverted Super Micro hardware to China. So what did those three months change in Super Micro Computer's business?

Super Micro Computer's Sales Jumped While Margins Slipped

Super Micro sold far more in fiscal Q1 2027, which ended September 30, than it did in the quarter before, but it kept less of each sale as gross profit. Revenue reached $19.9 billion, up 297.5% from a year earlier. During the November 3 call, management said about $2.3 billion of that total came from deployments first scheduled for earlier periods.

Gross margin fell to 12.7% from 17.5% in fiscal Q4 2026, though it remained higher than a year earlier, when it stood at 9.3%. AI solutions rose to about 71% of revenue from 59% in fiscal Q4 2026. Management named that mix as the key factor behind the lower margin, since gross margins are lower on large AI deployments than on its enterprise and channel business.

Is Super Micro Still Using Cash As It Grows?

Super Micro used $434 million of cash in its operations in fiscal Q1 2027, far less than the $6.8 billion it used in all of fiscal 2026, management said. Customers paying ahead of delivery helped, adding about $3.1 billion of deferred revenue in the quarter. In the last quarter of fiscal 2026, operations brought in $747 million. Over the twelve months to September 30, though, free cash flow was negative $6.5 billion, against net income of $3.66 billion, so the profit has not yet turned into cash.

More of the company's sales now come from one buyer. One large data center customer made up 44% of revenue in the quarter, against 28% for fiscal 2026 as a whole. Management expects that share to stay high while the build-outs run.

Where Super Micro's Profit And Sales Target Stand Now

Over the twelve months to September 30, Super Micro's operating margin was 8.6%, against 4.4% a year earlier. On November 3, management raised its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook to $72 billion to $82 billion, from $65 billion to $72 billion. Where the year lands in that range depends on how fast customers' data centers are ready and on the supply of key components, management said.

title: What Does SMCI Stock Offer That HP Does Not?

What Does SMCI Stock Offer That HP Does Not?

Image from Pixabay

Today's big story: Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash

HP (HPQ) offers one route into AI hardware, and Super Micro Computer provides another. HP delivers the technology to desks via its AI PCs and workstations, while Super Micro builds racks for AI data centers. Super Micro presents faster growth at a lower price, provided customers keep ordering and sales turn into cash. So is the demand behind Super Micro's sales still rising?

Super Micro Computer Has Raised Its Sales Outlook

So far, yes. On November 3, 2026, Super Micro raised its fiscal 2027 revenue outlook to $72 billion to $82 billion, from $65 billion to $72 billion. Management said the new range does not assume a repeat of the roughly $2.3 billion of delayed deliveries in fiscal Q1 2027. Demand remains concentrated, however: a single large data center customer made up 44% of that quarter's revenue.

HP's last outlook raise is a different kind. On August 26, 2026, HP raised its fiscal 2026 outlook for adjusted earnings per share to $3.19 to $3.29, from $2.90 to $3.10. It lifted its free cash flow outlook to $3 billion to $3.2 billion as well, yet management expected below-seasonal revenue in fiscal Q4 2026. Super Micro's raise is about how much it will sell, while HP's is about how much it will earn and keep. In September, though, HP warned that PC sales will drop through 2027, and it has since named Emma Walmsley as CEO.

Can Super Micro Computer Turn Its Sales Into Cash?

Not yet. Super Micro used $6.33 billion of cash in its operations over the four quarters ended September 30, 2026, while HP generated $4.67 billion over its four quarters ended July 31, 2026.

In fiscal Q1 2027 alone, Super Micro used $434 million on $19.9 billion of revenue, and management said customer prepayments funded most of its inventory build. The company also raised $5.6 billion in June to finance the working capital behind its orders.

HP hands its cash back instead, returning over $1.5 billion through dividends and buybacks in the first three quarters of fiscal 2026. Memory and storage costs show up in HP's margin. On its August call, management said it expected those costs to keep rising and its fiscal Q4 2026 margin to fall below its fiscal Q3 level.

How Do HP And Super Micro Computer Stack Up?

Super Micro trades as the cheaper stock, priced at 4.5 times trailing earnings at the November 16, 2026 close, against 10.7 for HP. Super Micro's revenue grew 156.5% over its four quarters ended September 30, 2026, compared with 8.1% for HP over its four quarters ended July 31, 2026. Super Micro also posted a wider operating margin over those periods, at 8.6% against 6.6% for HP. That growth has been uneven, however: in the twelve months ended September 30, 2025, Super Micro's revenue grew just 11.9%.

U.S. equity markets have witnessed heightened volatility in recent weeks amid a technology-led sell-off, concerns over Big Tech's massive artificial intelligence (AI) investments and stretched valuations. Political uncertainty following the midterm elections, persistent inflation, elevated Treasury yields and the Federal Reserve's hawkish monetary policy stance have further dampened investor sentiment. Fluctuating oil prices, tariff-related uncertainties and concerns over returns on AI infrastructure spending have intensified market turbulence. Nevertheless, resilient corporate earnings and intermittent market rebounds have helped equities retain their year-to-date gains, although investor confidence remains weak.

Hence, the traditional approach to stock selection remains a good idea. Sales growth offers a more reliable basis for evaluating stocks than earnings-focused metrics. In this regard, stocks like Super Micro Computer, Inc. SMCI, General Dynamics Corporation GD and Consolidated Edison, Inc. ED are worth betting on.

Sales growth is a key indicator of a company's operational strength, reflecting demand for its products and services and its ability to capitalize on market opportunities. Consistent revenue expansion often signals favorable industry trends, a growing customer base, market share gains, effective pricing strategies and successful business expansion. Higher sales can also improve operating leverage, supporting margin expansion and profitability.

However, assessing sales growth requires evaluating industry conditions, competitive positioning, pricing trends and macroeconomic factors. The sustainability and quality of revenue growth are equally important, as recurring revenues, strong customer retention and stable demand provide greater earnings visibility than temporary gains. Companies demonstrating consistent and sustainable sales growth are generally better positioned to generate robust cash flows, fund expansion initiatives, strengthen their competitive standing and create long-term shareholder value.

Selecting the Potential Winning Stocks

To shortlist stocks with impressive sales growth and a high cash balance, we have selected 5-Year Historical Sales Growth (%) greater than X-Industry and Cash Flow of more than $500 million as our main screening parameters.

But sales growth and cash strength are not the absolute criteria for selecting stocks. Hence, we have added other factors to arrive at a winning strategy.

P/S Ratio less than X-Industry: This metric determines the value placed on each dollar of a company's revenue. The lower the ratio, the better it is for picking a stock since the investor is paying less for each unit of sales.

% Change F1 Sales Estimate Revisions (four weeks) greater than X-Industry: Estimate revisions, better than the industry, are often seen to trigger an increase in stock price.

Operating Margin (average last five years) greater than 5%: The operating margin measures how much every dollar of a company's sales translates into profits. A high ratio indicates that the company has good cost control and sales are increasing faster than costs — an optimal situation.

Return on Equity (ROE) greater than 5%: This metric will ensure that sales growth is translated into profits and the company is not hoarding cash. A high ROE means that the company is spending wisely and is, in all likelihood, profitable.

Zacks Rank less than or equal to 2: Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) or 2 (Buy) stocks are known to outperform, irrespective of the market environment. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank stocks here.

Today's big story: Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash

More on the AI trade: our AI storyline page collects our pieces on AI stocks.

In November 2006, Nvidia made graphics chips for gamers and sold about $3 billion a year of them. Over the year to July 2026 it sold $303.0 billion, about 100 times as much, and its profit grew more than 400 times. $10,000 in its stock then is about $2.8 million now, against $76,000 for the same money in the S&P 500. Here is what that record teaches about this week. Nvidia reports third-quarter results after the close today, 35% below its October peak after another 4.1% drop on Monday.

Lesson 1: The Cash Spoke First

From fiscal 2006 through fiscal 2023, Nvidia brought in $42.6 billion of cash from operations against $34.6 billion of profit: $1.23 of cash for every dollar of profit. In that stretch only two profitable years came in below $1, the years to January 2019 and January 2022, and those years saw the start of its two biggest falls of the last decade, 56% and 66%.

Since then the cash has trailed profit three years running: 94 cents, then 88, then 86. Over the year to July: 70 cents. The record doesn't say a fall follows. It says this is the line that moved first before, and it is moving now. The full math is in today's big story, Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash.

Every dollar of that $2.8 million belonged to someone who sat through all three. Someone who bought at the 2007 peak waited eight and a half years to break even. The gains and the falls were the same stock; nobody got one without the other.

Would you have held through all three? Holding on is easier when your portfolio falls less than the market. For every dollar its benchmark lost, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio lost about 81 cents on average, holding 30 quality stocks in equal weight. See how HQ held up.

Lesson 3: The Risk You Didn't Choose

Suppose an investor put 5% of a portfolio in Nvidia in November 2006, the rest in the S&P 500, and never touched it. Today Nvidia would be about two-thirds of the portfolio. Winners grow into concentration on their own. Many investors also own Nvidia through index, tech and AI funds, where it is more than 6% of the S&P 500 and up to a fifth of some tech funds. The question for long-term holders this week isn't whether to sell Nvidia. It is whether today's size was ever a decision.
